sentences.text: Her grandmother read the stag the way other people read a barometer, which is to say quickly, without ceremony, and while doing something else.

They would be walking the top field in April and the stag would be at the far edge of the birches — he was always at the far edge of something, never in the open, never hidden — and her grandmother would glance over, and keep walking, and say something like *wet June* or *the pears will do nothing* and not mention it again.
Petra spent two summers assuming this was a joke that adults did.

She stopped assuming that in the August she was ten, when her grandmother looked at him across the stream in the second week of the month and stopped walking, which she never did, and stood there for a while.
"What?" "He's put on a fourth on the left." "So?" Her grandmother started walking again.

"So bring the ladder round on Thursday and we'll get the apples." They got the apples on the Thursday and Friday, all of them, three weeks earlier than any year Petra could remember, and everybody in the house complained about the work and about the apples being hard.
Her mother complained the loudest and complained for two days, and the complaint had a specific shape to it that Petra only understood later: it was not about the apples.
It was about being the household that did the strange thing, again, in a village where everybody could see the ladders from the road.
On the Sunday night the wind came in off the sea and took a dozen trees down along the river and stripped every orchard in the valley that had not been picked.
